messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ (variable) from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out, min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (average)
        *   $V_{out, max} \le 3.6\text{V}$
        *   Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$
        *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$
        *   Settled $\Delta V \le 0.02\text{V}$
    *   Piezo: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25nF) and 20M$\Omega$.
    *   Operating Conditions:
        *   S1: Nominal (Ip=50uA, f=100Hz, RL=330k)
        *   S2: Heavy load (RL=150k) -> $V_{out}$ might be too low.
        *   S3: Strong excitation, light load (Ip=100uA, RL=2200k) -> $V_{out}$ might be too high (over 3.6V).
        *   S4: Weak excitation (Ip=30uA, RL=1000k) -> $V_{out}$ might be too low.
        *   S5: Low freq (f=80Hz, RL=470k) -> Stability/settling issue.
        *   S6: High Temp/Cp (Cp=30nF, RL=330k).
    *    Reference Design (FBR):
        *   S1: Ok (mostly), but failed settled.
        *   S2: Fail ($V_{avg} = 1.76\text{V} < 1.8\text{V}$).
        *   S3: Fail ($V_{max} = 5.72\text{V} > 3.6\text{V}$, ripple too high).
        *   S4: Fail ($V_{avg} = 1.51\text{V} < 1.8\text{V}$).
        *   S5: Fail (settled).
        *   S6: Ok.

    *   The Full-Bridge Rectifier (FBR) is inefficient because of the diode drops and doesn't regulate voltage.
    *   Low $V_{oc}$ (3.2V) makes diode drops significant.
    *   S2 and S4 failures indicate the need for higher efficiency or voltage boosting.
    *   S3 failure indicates the need for voltage clamping/regulation.

    *   **Option 1: SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) / SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction).**
        *   SSHI can significantly increase harvested energy from piezo transducers by flipping the voltage across $C_p$.
        *   Basic SSHI: Inductor $L$ in series with a switch, triggered at peaks.
        *   For $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$, a standard FBR loses $2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$.
        *   SSHI-based converters can improve $V_{out}$ and efficiency.
    *   **Option 2: Active Rectification (Synchronous Rectifier).**
        *   Replacing diodes with switches. (However, we only have 4 switches and 2 SYNC controllers).
    *   **Option 3: Zener Clamp.**
        *   To solve S3 ($V_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$), a DZ33 (3.3V Zener) is essential.

    *   *Topology A: Parallel-SSHI (modified)*.
        *   Piezo $\to$ Full Bridge $\to$ Capacitor.
        *   But we need a boost mechanism.
        *   Wait, a simple and effective approach for low $V_{oc}$ is a "Buck-Boost" or a charge-pump, but we are limited to 16 components and SYNC controllers.
        *   SYNC controllers are ideal for SSHI.
        *   Standard SSHI: Piezo $\to$ Bridge $\to$ Out. Then a switch $S$ and inductor $L$ across the piezo to flip the voltage. But the prompt says SYNC closes switches at piezo voltage extrema.
        *   Let's try a "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) or "Parallel-SSHI" style.
        *   Actually, a simpler way to improve the FBR is to use the SYNC switches to implement a more efficient rectifier or a boost.
        *   Given the SYNC constraints (closes for $t_{on}$ at extrema), the most natural fit is an inductor-based inversion.
        *   *Proposed Structure 1: FBR + Zener + SSHI inversion.*
            *   Full Bridge (DSCH) for rectification.
            *   Storage Cap on "out".
            *   Zener DZ33 on "out" to clamp to 3.3V (fixes S3).
            *   SSHI circuit: Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
            *   SYNC triggers $S$ at peaks to flip $V_{Cp}$. This increases the energy extracted per cycle.

    *   *Topology B: SECE-like.*
        *   Instead of a full bridge, use switches to transfer charge.
        *   But with only 2 SYNC controllers, a full synchronous bridge is impossible.

    *   *Topology C: Half-bridge with clamp.*
        *   Standard half-bridge might not provide enough voltage.

    *   *Re-evaluating SSHI:*
        *   Piezo is between `pzp` and `pzn`.
        *   Full Bridge:
            *   D1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
            *   D2: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
            *   D3: `0` $\to$ `pzp`
            *   D4: `0` $\to$ `pzn`
        *   Storage: C1 (`out`, `0`).
        *   Clamp: D5 (`0`, `out`, DZ33).
        *   SSHI flip:
            *   L1: `pzp` $\to$ `n1`
            *   S1: `n1` $\to$ `pzn`
            *   Ctrl G1: `edges="both"`, `ton` calculated as $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
            *   This flips the voltage $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$ every half period.

    *   *Refining SSHI:*
        *   The FBR takes the current. The SSHI flip (L1, S1) happens at the peaks.
        *   Does this help $V_{out}$? Yes, it effectively increases the voltage seen by the rectifier.
        *   Wait, the FBR takes the current $I_p$. SSHI flips the voltage $V_{Cp}$. The energy extracted is $E = \frac{1}{2} C_p V_{peak}^2$. Without SSHI, we lose a lot. With SSHI, we can move the operating point.

    *   *Topology D: Simplified SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction).*
        *   SECE often uses an inductor and a switch to move charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.
        *   L1 between `pzp` and `n1`. S1 between `n1` and `out`.
        *   This might be too simple.

    *   *Checking Constraints again:*
        *   S2 and S4 are the killers ($V_{out} < 1.8\text{V}$).
        *   S3 is the other killer ($V_{out} > 3.6\text{V}$).
        *   FBR failed S2 and S4.
        *   SSHI increases the average DC voltage produced.
        *   A Zener DZ33 is mandatory for S3.

    *   *Proposed Design 1 (SSHI + FBR + Zener):*
        *   Rectification: 4x DSCH (Full Bridge).
        *   Storage: C (`out`, `0`).
        *   Clamp: DZ33 (`0`, `out`).
        *   Inversion: L (`pzp`, `n1`), S (`n1`, `pzn`), SYNC (both edges).

    *   *Proposed Design 2 (Half-Bridge + Zener + SSHI):*
        *   Half-bridge might be too low voltage, but more efficient.
        *   Let's stick to the FBR as the base and add SSHI.

    *   *Proposed Design 3 (Inductor-based Boost / Charge Pump):*
        *   Use the SYNC switch to create a boost.
        *   L between `pzp` and `n1`. S between `n1` and `out`.
        *   When S closes, $C_p$ charges L. When S opens, L discharges into `out` via a diode.
        *   D (`n1`, `out`).
        *   This is a basic boost converter driven by the piezo frequency.

    *   L value: $\pi \sqrt{L C_p} \approx 30\text{--}50\text{ $\mu$s}$. For $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, $L \approx 10\text{--}100\text{ $\mu$H}$.
    *   Wait, the prompt says $L$ is $1\text{e-05}$ to $0.01\text{H}$ ($10\text{ $\mu$H}$ to $10\text{mH}$). $10\text{ $\mu$H}$ is available.
    *   C storage: $2.2\text{ $\mu$F}$ was used in FBR. Maybe $10\text{ $\mu$F}$ for better ripple? $4.7\text{ $\mu$F}$ is the max.

    *   *Design 1: FBR + Zener + SSHI*
        *   D1: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (DSCH)
        *   D2: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (DSCH)
        *   D3: `0` $\to$ `pzp` (DSCH)
        *   D4: `0` $\to$ `pzn` (DSCH)
        *   D5: `0` $\to$ `out` (DZ33)
        *   C1: `out` $\to$ `0` (2.2uF)
        *   L1: `pzp` $\to$ `n1` (100uH)
        *   S1: `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
        *   G1: SYNC (both edges, ton=30us)

    *   *Design 2: SECE (Simplified)*
        *   SECE transfers $C_p$ energy to $C_{out}$ using an inductor.
        *   L1: `pzp` $\to$ `n1`
        *   S1: `n1` $\to$ `out`
        *   D1: `n1` $\to$ `out` (This isn't quite right).
        *   Let's try a standard SECE:
            *   D1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
            *   S1: `pzp` $\to$ `n1`
            *   L1: `n1` $\to$ `out`
            *   (This is getting complex).

    *   *Design 3: Optimized FBR + Zener* (Maybe the FBR just needed better components or the Zener?)
        *   Actually, the reference design was just FBR.
        *   Let's try a "Voltage Doubler" if $V_{oc}$ is low.
        *   But the $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$ peak. $V_{avg}$ for a rectifier is $2/\pi \times 3.2 \approx 2.0\text{V}$.
        *   With diode drops, it drops to $\sim 1.5\text{V}$, explaining S2 and S4 failures.
        *   SSHI is the best way to raise the average voltage.

    *   Let's focus on SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor).
    *   The basic SSHI circuit:
        *   Rectifier (FBR) provides the path to the load.
        *   An inductor-switch branch in parallel with the piezo flips the voltage.
    *   Wait, there's a "Parallel-SSHI" and "Series-SSHI".
    *   In Parallel-SSHI, the inductor-switch is in parallel with the piezo.
    *   Connectivity:
        *   Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   S1: `pzp` $\to$ `n1`
        *   L1: `n1` $\to$ `pzn`
        *   Rectifier:
            *   D1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
            *   D2: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
            *   D3: `0` $\to$ `pzp`
            *   D4: `0` $\to$ `pzn`
        *   C1: `out` $\to$ `0`
        *   D5: `0` $\to$ `out` (DZ33)

    *   S2: Heavy load (150k). $V_{out}$ was 1.76V (FBR). SSHI should push it above 1.8V.
    *   S3: Strong excitation. $V_{out}$ was 5.72V. Zener DZ33 will clamp it to $\sim 3.3\text{V}$.
    *   S4: Weak excitation. $V_{out}$ was 1.51V. SSHI should help.
    *   Startup: $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$. $2.2\text{ $\mu$F}$ might be too slow to charge? Maybe $1\text{ $\mu$F}$? Let's stick to $2.2\text{ $\mu$F}$ or let the optimizer handle it.
    *   Ripple: $0.05\text{V}$. $C_{out}$ must be large enough.

    *   The SYNC closes at "voltage extrema". This is perfect for flipping the voltage across $C_p$.
    *   $L$ and $C_p$ form a resonant circuit. $\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC_p}$. Half a period is $\pi \sqrt{LC_p}$.
    *   $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{LC_p}$.
    *   For $C_p = 25\text{nF}$ and $L = 1\text{mH}$, $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{1\text{e-3} \cdot 25\text{e-9}} \approx 15.7\text{ $\mu$s}$.
    *   Wait, $L$ can be up to $10\text{mH}$. $t_{on}$ can be up to $1\text{ms}$.

    *   Design 1: FBR + Zener + SSHI (Parallel).
    *   Design 2: Half-Bridge (two diodes) + Zener + SSHI. (Half-bridge is more efficient but gives half the voltage. With SSHI, maybe it's enough?)
    *   Actually, let's try one more: a "Charge Pump" style.
    *   But SSHI is the gold standard for this.

    *Let's double-check the "both" edges for SYNC.*
    - At positive peak: $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$ is max positive. S1 closes, L1-C_p resonate, $V$ flips to negative.
    - At negative peak: $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$ is max negative. S1 closes, L1-C_p resonate, $V$ flips to positive.
    - This keeps the piezo voltage always "pushing" through the rectifier.

    *Let's refine the FBR diodes:*
    - D1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
    - D2: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
    - D3: `0` $\to$ `pzp`
    - D4: `0` $\to$ `pzn`
    - Wait, the standard full bridge is:
      - `pzp` $\to$ `out` (D1)
      - `pzn` $\to$ `out` (D2)
      - `0` $\to$ `pzp` (D3)
      - `0` $\to$ `pzn` (D4)
      - This means when `pzp` is positive, D1 and D4 conduct. When `pzp` is negative, D2 and D3 conduct. This is correct.

    *One more thing:* The Zener DZ33 should be cathode at `out`, anode at `0`.
    - `["0", "out"]` $\to$ Anode `0`, Cathode `out`. Correct.

    *Wait, the prompt mentions "return diodes have their anode on ground".*
    - `["0", "pzp"]` $\to$ Anode `0`, Cathode `pzp`. Correct.

    *Let's refine the SSHI switch connectivity:*
    - L1: `pzp` $\to$ `n1`
    - S1: `n1` $\to$ `pzn`
    - This puts the L-S branch in parallel with the piezo.

    *Wait, will the SSHI current bypass the rectifier?*
    - The SSHI switch only closes for a few microseconds. Most of the time, the current goes through the rectifier. This is how it's supposed to work.

    *What about the $t_{on}$ and $L$ values?*
    - $L = 1\text{mH}$
    - $C_p = 25\text{nF}$
    - $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{1\text{e-3} \cdot 25\text{e-9}} = 15.7\text{ $\mu$s}$.
    - I'll propose $L=1\text{mH}, t_{on}=15\text{ $\mu$s}$.

    - FBR: 4 diodes (DSCH).
    - Zener: 1 diode (DZ33).
    - SSHI: 1 inductor (L), 1 switch (S), 1 SYNC (G1).
    - Storage: 1 capacitor (C).
    - Total: 8 components. (Limit is 16).

    - S2 (150k load) needs more power. SSHI increases the voltage delivered to the cap, and the rectifier will deliver more current.
    - S3 (Strong exc, 2200k load) will be clamped by DZ33.
    - S4 (Weak exc) will be boosted by SSHI.
    - Ripple: $C_{out} = 2.2\text{ $\mu$F}$ might be enough, but we can go up to $4.7\text{ $\mu$F}$. Let's use $2.2\text{ $\mu$F}$ as a starting point for the optimizer.

    *One detail:* Does the SSHI flip happen at the right time?
    - SYNC closes at "piezo voltage extrema". For a current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ in parallel with $C_p$, the voltage is $V = \int (I_p \sin(\omega t) / C_p) dt = - (I_p / \omega C_p) \cos(\omega t)$.
    - Extrema are at $t = 0, \pi/\omega, 2\pi/\omega...$
    - This is exactly when we want to flip.

    *Is there any other topology?*
    - Maybe a "Synchronous Rectifier" using the 2 SYNC controllers?
    - SYNC1 for the positive half, SYNC2 for the negative half.
    - S1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`, S2: `pzn` $\to$ `out`, S3: `0` $\to$ `pzp`, S4: `0` $\to$ `pzn`.
    - But we only have 2 SYNC controllers. We can't control 4 switches independently unless we group them.
    - G1 (edges="pos") controls S1 and S4.
    - G2 (edges="neg") controls S2 and S3.
    - This would be a fully synchronous rectifier! It's much more efficient than DSCH.
    - Let's try this as Design 2.

    *Design 2: Fully Synchronous Rectifier + Zener.*
    - S1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`, ctrl: G1
    - S2: `pzn` $\to$ `out`, ctrl: G2
    - S3: `0` $\to$ `pzp`, ctrl: G2
    - S4: `0` $\to$ `pzn`, ctrl: G1
    - G1: edges="pos", ton=1ms (just to keep it closed for the whole half-cycle).
    - G2: edges="neg", ton=1ms.
    - Zener: `0` $\to$ `out` (DZ33).
    - Storage: `out` $\to$ `0` (C).
    - This removes the diode drops entirely (Ron = 2 Ohm).
    - This should be very efficient for S2 and S4.

    *Wait, can the switches stay closed for $1\text{ms}$?*
    - "ton: 1e-07..0.001". Yes, $1\text{ms}$ is the max.
    - Period $T = 1/100 = 10\text{ms}$. Half-period is $5\text{ms}$.
    - $t_{on} = 1\text{ms}$ is not enough to cover the whole half-period.
    - The switches will only be closed for $1\text{ms}$ at the peak. This is actually just a sampled-data rectifier.
    - That's not good. The diodes are better for the continuous part.

    *Back to Design 1 (SSHI + FBR).* It's a robust and well-known improvement.
    *What about a modified SSHI where the switch is not in parallel with the piezo, but in the rectifier path?*
    - No, let's stick to the standard.

    *Let's try Design 3: A simple Boost converter using the SYNC.*
    - L1: `pzp` $\to$ `n1`
    - S1: `n1` $\to$ `0` (ctrl: G1)
    - D1: `n1` $\to$ `out` (DSCH)
    - G1: edges="both", ton=...
    - When S1 closes, L1 charges from $C_p$. When S1 opens, L1 dumps into `out` through D1.
    - This is essentially a boost converter. It might be more efficient than FBR.
    - But it only uses one polarity of the piezo.
    - We could add another branch for the negative polarity.
    - L2: `pzn` $\to$ `n2`, S2: `n2` $\to$ `0` (ctrl: G2), D2: `n2` $\to$ `out`.
    - This uses 2 SYNC controllers, 2 Switches, 2 Inductors, 2 Diodes.
